utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today, we are Tuesday, the 11th of December -- the 11th of December, 2007. I'd like to greet all the people present in the courtroom, Mrs. Dahl, Mr. Seselj, as well as all the people in this courtroom and those people assisting us in our job. Today we have a witness who is due to testify for two days. Today it will be the turn of the Prosecutor for her examination-in-chief, and tomorrow it will be the turn of Mr. Seselj for his cross-examination. Let me remind you that initially the Prosecution had filed a motion for this witness to be considered as an expert witness. The Trial Chamber handed down a decision on the matter recently and decided that this witness would be heard as a mere witness and not as any other witness, pursuant to Rule 94 bis, and in light of our decision, the Prosecution has disclosed additional information to us, thereby substantiating the fact that this witness has enough knowledge to qualify as an expert witness. The Trial Chamber, after hearing the witness's testimony, will decide on what decision to take vis-a-vis the report of this witness and what probative value should be granted to this witness and his report after having heard all questions and answers. I would like the usher to introduce the witness now, please. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. Before you bring this witness in, may I inform you that I have never received your decision to the effect that this witness will be heard as an ordinary witness, rather than as an expert witness. For two years now I've been preparing for this witness as an expert witness for the Prosecution, and it is only on that basis that it makes sense for this witness to testify. This witness was not present during any one of my crimes or anything that other people did under my influence allegedly. He has nothing to testify unless he is an expert. He cannot testify about my books. He hasn't read them. He's only been shown fragments of my book. I think this is a very important question, and it has to be dealt with before the witness appears in court. I am prepared to hear this witness as an expert. If you want to take me by surprise now that he was some kind of an eyewitness of some crimes of mine, then I'm not prepared for that, because I don't know what crimes we're talking about, what it is that he could testify about here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I discover now that you have not had the decision handed down by the Chamber on the 30th of November, 2007. I'm very surprised by this, because we did give an instruction to that effect. Let me then just read out part of this decision, as well as its disposition, so that you are able to understand what was stipulated in this decision. The Trial Chamber in its decision recalls that the Trial Chamber, in light of its discretion, can, namely, refer to the resume, publications, and any other information relating to the witness when this witness qualifies as an expert. The Trial Chamber has referred to the expert report entitled "Nationalist Propaganda of Vojislav Seselj, Technical Contact, Impact," and the Table of Contents, which provides an explanation as to what kind of methodology has been used. Considered that the subject addressed in this report, the Trial Chamber feels that the field of expertise of Mr. Oberschall should be as follows: Mass media propaganda in general; and more specifically, in Serbia, nationalist propaganda of the accused. Given that in a number of articles written by Anthony Oberschall, some relate to the former Yugoslavia and violence in the Balkans, but these articles are of a general nature. They do not seem to tie into the expertise of the witness in question. Given that Anthony Oberschall does not seem to have any technical experience of the former Yugoslavia or that he has any knowledge of the social and cultural background of the region; quite the contrary. The presence of an interpreter or translator demonstrates that Mr. Oberschall worked on an English text where each word has been translated, and it's important to put this in the right context. The Trial Chamber therefore feels that Mr. Oberschall cannot testify as an expert witness pursuant to 94 bis relating to those issues addressed. However, this Trial Chamber feels this testimony should not be disregarded, in light of the indictment, and decides to hear Mr. Oberschall as a Prosecution witness, given that the Prosecution nonetheless has identified prior to its examination the field or the questions put to the witness. Therefore, the expert report, in addition to both addenda, be tendered into evidence wholly or in part, follow the same criteria as those applied to any other exhibit. Therefore, the Trial Chamber orders Mr. Oberschall to be heard before the Chamber as a Prosecution witness, to be examined by the parties and the Bench. The Prosecution has identified clearly its series of questions by disclosing to the Chamber and to the accused before the 7th of December a list of topics on which Mr. Oberschall will testify by stipulating the number of pages -- pages, reference number, and excerpts which will be referred to and that have been studied by Mr. Oberschall as part of the examination-in-chief. This disposition was rendered on the 30th of November, 2007. The examination-in-chief should be no longer than three hours and 45 minutes. The accused will have the same time. After that, the Trial Chamber has sent to the Prosecution - you should have received this document too - which clearly indicated which topics would be addressed by the Prosecution. This was a request put in by the Bench. The Bench wished to have reference numbers and document numbers. This is something which has certainly been translated and disclosed to you. Mrs. Dahl, have you sent Mr. Seselj the document which you sent to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we made special arrangements at the Detention Unit to have the material presented to Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So if I've understood you correctly, on the basis of this document, you are going to address issues of methodology, terminology, collective violence, the former Yugoslavia, effects of propaganda on the masses, and so on and so forth. All these items listed in this document. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, so have you had this document or haven't you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Judge, I have not received this document. The Prosecution submitted to me only comments and replies of Anthony Oberschall to my opening statement that I made on the 8th of November before this Trial Chamber. And in view of my first official notification concerning the Prosecution witness on the 23rd of August, 2006. I had no idea about the status of this expert being changed. I had the right to request certification for -- to appeal, but I have been denied this right because I have not received this decision. In a word, I am astonished. I wanted to challenge this expert precisely through similar words, as the Trial Chamber challenged him, what you read out now from the decision of the Trial Chamber, a few of my own arguments. You see? Now I have to question this man about different matters, and he cannot be a witness to anything. Perhaps he is a reader of fragments of my books. He has not read a single book of mine. He's only read fragments that somebody else has prepared for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are making a mistake. You are prepared to hear him on the basis of the report that has been prepared by the witness. The Prosecution, pursuant to the decision rendered by the Trial Chamber, has prepared its examination-in-chief on the basis of the report of the expert. But just to make quite sure that everybody understands, the Trial Chamber has asked the Prosecution to map its examination-in-chief out in order to highlight a number of issues which are already contained in his report. It's the order in which these topics which will be addressed. It's just a way of understanding in which order this will unfold. Therefore, your preparation stands as is. Nothing has been changed. The only issue which the Chamber at the end of the day will have to determine is to know whether, because you did challenge the quality of this expert. You challenged the content of his report. And therefore, the only matter to determine is whether what the expert is going to tell us is true or not, whether it is useful in light of the indictment, and whether it seems that what the expert is telling us when he answers the questions put to him by the Prosecution and the questions that will be put by you, whether any of this has a probative value. And this can only be determined right at the end, after these two days. It is impossible right now to say whether the man who is going to testify today is a real expert or whether what he is about to say or will say is of any interest and whether this fits in with the definition of the term. Therefore, we will now bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to say something else before you bring the witness in. As for this last thing you said, I completely agree with that, Judge. However, there is one thing that I do oppose: If this witness fails as an expert in the courtroom, his testimony cannot be treated as testimony by an ordinary witness. He failed as an expert, and he -- and he leaves the courtroom shamed because he did not manage to prove anything as an expert. If he manages to prove something as an expert, then I failed. However, for you to re-qualify him as an ordinary witness if he fails as an expert witness, that would be totally wrong. I do not mind having him heard today as a Prosecution witness in chief, and I will cross-examine him tomorrow as a Prosecution expert. And finally you will rule whether you accept him as an expert or not. However, if you do not accept him as an expert, then he amounts to zero. You cannot turn him into something else. He cannot be turned into an ordinary witness in any way. Another thing, Judge: I would like to draw your attention to the fact that there are enormous problems with the translation service. I made two submissions to you, and my associates analysed the translations into English and French. Both are disastrous and both are incorrect tendentiously. If you do not change this translation service, if you do not get rid of incompetent translators, then your transcripts will be no good. I make an enormous effort to engage good translators, proper translators, so that they will translate the transcripts of these proceedings to me subsequently. I mentioned all of that to you in two submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second item you have addressed, we will look into it; namely, the quality of the translation. I would like to ask the Registrar why the documents provided by the Prosecution have not been addressed to Mr. Seselj. And secondly, why the decision of the Trial Chamber relating to the quality of Mr. Oberschall's report on the 30th of November, 2007 - that's more than ten days ago - has not been translated and addressed to Mr. Seselj. Mr. Seselj, now, as far as the expert is concerned, let me remind you that initially the Prosecution filed a motion to -- with a view to asking Mr. Oberschall's report to be considered as an expert report, pursuant to Rule 94 bis of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence. You challenged the entire report as well as the quality of expert of the person in question pursuant to the procedure which you are entitled to apply. Paragraph (B) of 94(B)(iii). And let me read it out to you. You know it as well as I do. If you are to challenge the quality of a expert witness or the relevance of the report or the statements wholly or in part, you must then indicate which are the challenged parts. So according to Rule 94 bis, you are entitled to challenge this, in light of the motion, in light of the report, in light of your submissions, the Trial Chamber has decided that as things stand, it cannot say that this gentleman could be deemed to be an expert witness, in the general sense of the term. But the Trial Chamber, when it rendered its decision, stayed its decision on the issue of admitting the report. And if you don't know anything about this, let me indicate this to you. When an expert is brought in, this expert is heard, and at the end of the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination the Trial Chamber then decides whether the report should be admitted or not. And in certain cases, some Trial Chambers have not admitted the reports. It depends on the questions and answers, and sometimes it may happen that during the hearing, the so-called expert witness was in fact not an expert witness. And in that case, the Trial Chamber decides not to admit the report, which, of course, cuts down on the time or cuts down on the testimony of the expert. Perhaps the Trial Chamber will admit this report or perhaps it won't admit the report. Much will depend on how the questions are put by the Prosecution and how you are going to put your questions. It is only then that the Trial Chamber will decide whether to admit this report or not. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully agree, Judge. All of that is fine. However, there is one thing I do oppose: If you decide in the end that the report of this expert is not admitted and if he turns into an ordinary witness, I think that is impossible. If the report is not admitted as an expert report, then it failed. That is a victory of mine then in this specific case. After that, his testimony cannot be treated in any way whatsoever. He leaves the courtroom defeated and that's it. He cannot be an ordinary witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are quite right when you say that if he has failed. Those are your own words. In that case, the Trial Chamber will not take this into consideration. In that case, the Trial Chamber will not refer to the testimony in any way. However, if the report is admitted, then the Trial Chamber will refer to it. So there is no contradiction here between what the Trial Chamber holds and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Mrs. Dahl, you'd like to respond to what Mr. Seselj has just said?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. At this point, I consider the matter an academic matter. The test under Rule 89(C) is that the Chamber may admit any evidence it deems to have relevance and probative value. There's no higher or different threshold for testimony provided by expert witnesses. This is the standard articulated in the decision of 30 November, and we will present the Chamber with information on which it can determine whether Dr. Oberschall has the -- met the criteria under Rule 94 bis; namely, whether he has specialised skill or training that can aid the Chamber in trying the facts of this case to understand or determine disputed issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So let us bring in the witness now, please. Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more thing, by your leave. By your leave, just one more thing, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not against the Trial Chamber assessing the probative value of any testimony, but please tell me about this alleged expert. If he fails as an expert here, how can he be treated as an ordinary witness? That is inconceivable. That is absolutely impossible. That is the essence of my objection. Otherwise, I've prepared for his expert report. No stone will remain unturned. But how can he be treated as an ordinary witness once he fails as an expert? That's the only thing that I consider to be in dispute. That is impossible for the Trial Chamber to do. Everything else is quite possible. I don't mind having this alleged expert brought in and the cross-examination in chief started; however, what is absolutely impossible is to treat him as an ordinary witness once he fails as an expert. According to Rule 89(F), a Chamber may receive the evidence of witness orally or where interests of justice allow, written form, but it has to be probative value. It's not somebody reading fragments from my books and then making his own comments with regard to these fragments. That has no probative value. Everyone knows what probative value is. There has to be authentic evidence so that it could have probative value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have noted what you have said, and the Trial Chamber will assess all of this in light of the questions and answers and in light of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. I just want to check that you can hear in your own language the translation of what I'm saying. If that is the case, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I can hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Sir, to take the solemn declaration, I would like you to stand, please. First of all, for the transcript, please give me your first name, last name, and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anthony Oberschall. December 4, 1936.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am retired, emeritus professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, USA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, have you already testified before a court on the events that unfolded in the former Yugoslavia, or is it the first time you testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Prosecution, I would just like to share with you some information. The Prosecution has asked you to come and testify, to testify on a number of issues which could help the Chamber to better understand this case. The Trial Chamber has been seized of this case, as you know. As we are in an adversarial system, as you know, you will first be asked to answer the questions that will be put to you by Mrs. Dahl in the course of this morning's hearing, and she will also show you a number of documents. After this, Mr. Seselj, the accused, who is sitting on your left, will spend tomorrow's hearing cross-examining you. Before you, the members of the Bench can step in at any time if they wish to put questions to you relating to the documents or relating to any questions you may have provided to one or other party. We have 20-minute breaks every hour and a half, and as we started as 9.00, we shall have a break at 10.30, have a 20-minute break, and then resume until quarter to 2.00. If at any point in time you wish to interrupt the hearing, do not hesitate to do so. And we will then, of course, interrupt the hearing if you feel uncomfortable about something. So this is how this hearing will unfold. Please try to provide brief and accurate answers. If you do not understand a question, please do not hesitate to turn to the person who has put the question to you to rephrase it. Mrs. Dahl, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Oberschall?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: First, I would like to address some questions to you concerning your qualifications as an expert about the manipulation of public opinion through propaganda and the propaganda methods used by Serbian political leaders, in particular Dr. Oberschall -- I mean, excuse me, Dr. Seselj. What is your professional training?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: I'm a Ph.D. in sociology, and I've been a university professor for 40 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What area do you teach?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: I teach political sociology, social movements, war and peace studies, in particular areas such as the -- Eastern Europe and the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Have you published books or articles concerning conflict and peace building?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Yes. In March of this year, I had a book published, which is called "Conflict and Peacebuilding in Divided Societies. Responses to Ethnic Violence." And of the seven chapters, there's a whole chapter devoted to the break-up of Yugoslavia and especially the Bosnian war and the Dayton Peace Agreement and its following events.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What work did you conduct to write that book?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Well, that took really about -- it's the culmination of about 15 years of work on not just the Bosnian and the Yugoslav case but certainly that was a very central part of it. I took three field trips. In addition to the archival work, documents, historical research, looking at all the United Nations papers and results, I took three field trips to former Yugoslavia. The first one in 1998, and I did interviews with a number of people from political leaders, media, personnel, refugees, actually in Belgrade, Sarajevo, Banja Luka, Bihac, Zagreb, and probably some other places I don't quite remember and this took about three weeks. Then I had another field trip in 2001, in the area. And just last year I had another two-week research trip with some Balkan graduate students in Bosnia to study the reconstruction after the war and this was a project run out of Trento University, I mean, Trento University invited me to try to get a grant for this research which I was successful in obtaining. And so I have a continued interest, actually, more now on the peace-building side than on the conflict side, but I started --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Just a minute. We have a problem. We don't have a transcript anymore. The registrar needs to bring in a technician. Mrs. Dahl, please put your question again because it hasn't been recorded on the transcript. No, we don't have it. So let's try again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Should I go ahead?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Seemingly it's working again.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Well, let me return to the topic of my last question. I wanted to present to the Chamber information about the research and field studies that you have conducted in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What university gave you -- or what -- with what university were you doing work for Balkan reconstruction and redevelopment in 2006?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Well, in 2006 the University of Trento has a -- a programme in the Balkans on development and -- and reconstruction, and they -- they needed, so to say, an outsider to come in and organise the -- the intellectual and the research part of it, which I did. We obtained a grant from the Erasmus fund of the European Union, went to Trento, and ended up with about two weeks of -- of field work to -- to get the students started in -- in Bosnia. I myself did interviews in -- in Sarajevo and Bihac. Actually, these are people I interviewed already in 1998 and then in -- and some of them in 2001. And I get some information on them, on what the changes are. And this -- this research project has then continued. I mean, I was there just to get it started for them. And I'm retired now and I do other things. But I thought it was very -- it was something that I -- because of what I know, I'm very happy to do, even though I'm retired.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Where is University of Trento?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: University of Trento is in Northern Italy. It is a very well-known university.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Have you published articles in professional journals on the manipulation of ethnicity with regard to violence and war in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Well, the major one that I published was -- I think it was 2000, the year 2000, and it was in the journal called "Racial and ethnic studies," which, by the way, is the -- is internationally known for -- where is my vitae here? Oh, here. This is really the premier international journal on the topic of ethnic relations, ethnic studies. And it has been reprinted and referred to a number of times. And the title of it is "From ethnic cooperation to violence and war" in -- no, it's called -- that is another one. It's "The manipulation of ethnicity from cooperation to violence and war in Yugoslavia." And it was published in 2000, November 2000.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: When you're doing your original research in the region of the former Yugoslavia, how do you talk with people? What languages do you use, and do you use translators?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I always have a -- usually a university student, sometimes a -- a high school -- you know, late high school student. But it turns out, for instance, that -- I happen to speak French and German fluently, and actually I learned those languages before I learned English, because my family immigrated to the United States when I was 15. So in Belgrade the intellectuals and academics actually speak French, so we were able to -- to speak French with one another. In Bosnia and Croatia, the -- not just the intellectuals but some of the, I should say, average, ordinary people often speak German, because they were labour migrants in Germany, so in that case sometimes I could speak German with them. They would understand it and they would answer in, you know, Serbo-Croatian and then that would be translated to me, but sometimes I could just speak with them in German. And some of the younger people actually speak English pretty well. And when I didn't have any common language I could speak with them, I used my interpreters. And that -- to me, that worked very well, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What were you asked to do in connection with the case against Dr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: I was asked to content analyse his -- well, what was in these -- this collection of volumes that -- that he himself, I think, edited or somebody in Belgrade edited, which contained not just writings but transcripts of TV interviews, radio interviews, speeches he made in the Serb Assembly, and, you know, other such material, for the period 1991-1994, and especially looking at the discourse that he had on Serb/non-Serb political relations, which is the, if you wish, nationalist discourse that -- that he conducted during this time of 1991-1994, and making sure that we captured both the TV, radio, as well as the -- the written material and speeches to the Assembly so that we wouldn't miss a particular audience that he was addressing.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now, before we talk about the methodology of content analysis --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: -- I would like to ask you some questions about the nature of the texts you were reading and the degree of difficulty in interpreting or understanding the material with the use of translated material. Were you able to understand what Mr. Seselj was saying in his political discourse?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Well, I had a Miss Bela Maric, who is a native Serbo-Croat speaker, who was at that time a graduate student in Slavic languages and also a candidate for Ph.D. in linguistics, which is a very nice combination to have somebody in the language literature and the linguistics field. And she is the one who actually translated for me the text that I content analysed. Now, these texts were extremely straightforward. There's nothing very subtle about nationalist discourse. You know, we're not translating the poetry of Baudelaire or anything like that. And things like "amputate Croatia" is really what it says. I mean, it's very vivid, it's clear. There's no subtle double meanings to it. So the only thing that Ms. Bela Maric did is she sometimes told me some details about the -- the context and the history which would explain better the actual -- you know, the actual text and -- and -- and what was referred to. And it went very smoothly. I had no problem whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm going to leave a pause between my question and your answer now, because I want to make sure the interpreters are able to follow us.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: When I reviewed your report, I noticed that you cited scholars and politicians who wrote about the conflict and conducted their own research in the region. Is that -- did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Why did you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection, Your Honour. Mr. President. Do you allow me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor must not ask leading questions of the witness, like with any other witness in chief examination. The Prosecutor cannot note something or make a statement and then say "am I right?" Questions must be: How, where, when. Questions must be direct, not leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mrs. Dahl. In examination-in-chief, Mrs. Dahl, you know that there can be no leading questions. And where you're saying "do I understand you right," this is calling for a specific answer, and he does answer "yes." That's on line 22, page 19. So could you please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What scholars and politicians did you consult in educating yourself and preparing your research analysis with regard to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Well, they are in the citations to my expert report. These are the -- the main sources and the main authorities that have discussed the whole Yugoslav break-up and the Yugoslav question and the history of Yugoslavia, and so on. During this decade, I went to many conferences, at which I met some of them. Some of them I know personally and referred to their -- their work. And if I can just explain a little bit that social science -- I mean, what we know about both the case of the break-up of Yugoslavia and what we know about mass communications and propaganda and persuasion, persuasion techniques, and so on, is a -- is not something that I invented. It's a -- it's a huge edifice made up of many different bricks that have been built into a pretty impressive building that I call "knowledge," and what I'm doing is I'm referring to the main building blocks, just the way Your Honours, the Judges, would look at particular precedents in the law that have been made over a number of years and maybe in different countries on a certain topic and you base your judgement on this particular edifice made up of many bricks, and social science is exactly the same way. So that is what I have done by referring to these sources in the citations. Plus, there was some research going on in -- actually, in -- in Serbia on content analysis of the media, on commentaries, on -- on the very same topics that I am covering, and I felt that I should -- you should cite them. In most cases, they -- they agree and I agree with them, and they agree with my conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you give me a summary of the conclusions that you reached after reviewing the writings and speeches of Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: If -- I think it's maybe appropriate at this point if I give you some -- some idea, some concrete idea of the -- the kind of nationalist discourse that Dr. Seselj engaged in, which is based on the -- on the content analysis. And I'm trying to locate this here. Well, okay, let me just -- I can't find the exact passage, so I'm just going to paraphrase myself. But in terms of looking at the speeches and other pronouncements of -- of Dr. Seselj on Serb/non-Serb relations, political relations, the content of it, both in terms of the themes that he covers and in terms of the techniques that he uses, is an extreme -- it's extreme nationalism. I call it "xenophobic nationalism." It's repeated over and over again. It doesn't really change over the years that I've looked at or over the -- the particular audience or the media that I've -- that I examined. It consists of several elements that I've -- that I've coded for, that I hope we get into the details of. But essentially the speech, typical Seselj's discourse, will start with a glorification of the Serbs, that they're -- they're sort of a great people, they have been victimised. There's a victimisation component to this speech. They have been victimised. They have all these external enemies. They are, in fact, internal enemies to the Serbs. They have been wronged in past history and in the present. Furthermore, they are threatened, again, by a combination of external enemies and internal -- internal enemies; and that the reaction to these threats is to take action and eliminate the source of the threat by aggressive and -- and violent means. The -- the solutions he proposes to the -- to Serb/non-Serb relations broke -- admit of no compromise, and even though he says that it's better to have a non-violent kind of an outcome, the outcome that he suggests to the adversary is one that -- that he advocates without any kind of a compromise solution to it. And absent and -- some kind of a total submission of the adversary to this notion of the Greater Serbia and as a successor to the -- to the Yugoslav state why aggressive violent means are -- are appropriate and should be undertaken. And those means involve not just armed conflict but ethnic cleansing and annexation of major parts of Croatia and perhaps other parts of -- of ex-Yugoslavia to -- to Serbia. And essentially that gives you an idea of the -- the content that I derived from this examination of his -- of some 400 different texts of Seselj discourse from 1991 to 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, just a question, a follow-up question after what you just said, which seems to sum up your entire report. Listening to you closely, you told us how exacerbated nationalism could manifest itself, through glorification of the Serbs as a great people, the fact that they were victims, enemies, internal enemies, external enemies, and that action was absolutely required, without accepting any kind of compromise, and that in terms of action, you determined the two kinds of actions that were envisaged; notably, ethnic cleansing. Very well. This is the way you see things. But as a Judge, this is the question that comes to my mind: What exactly is the difference with the traditional political discourse that is heard everywhere. And I'm not going to quote anyone, but everyone will have somebody in mind. So what exactly is the difference between a traditional political discourse that an everyday politician will give and what you have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm glad you asked the question. The -- in political science, there is -- and in fact, in public speaking, there's a discourse called "deliberative discourse." And deliberative discourse is what takes place in legislatures, such as the British Parliament and any kind of public debate in -- in Western democracies that, in fact, has been studied with content analysis, and there's a whole literature on this. And if you look at the coding categories that I use by my colleagues who studied this deliberative discourse and if you look at, as I have done, in textbooks on public speaking -- for instance, at my university, we teach public speaking and textbooks are used. And if you look at the Table of Content, you don't -- you find no entry for threat, for fear, for revenge and retribution. And -- and a number of these categories that in a nationalist, especially the xenophobic nationalist discourse and propaganda analysis that has been done during and after World War II on both the Nazi and allied propaganda, for instance. These are very different themes in these two kinds of discourse. And the difference between propaganda and this deliberative discourse, if I can just read a definition of "propaganda": "Propaganda is an endeavour to spread ideas without regard to truth and accuracy." And, in fact, full of threats and other rhetorical and other devices that would make people anxious, afraid, and hostile and mistrustful of -- of one another. So the difference between what I examined in Dr. Seselj's discourse and what my colleague Jurg Steiner, who does the analysis of the discourse in European Parliaments, is that we're sort of living in somewhat two different worlds of discourse. Now, there are some politicians who are using a kind of in-between, Hugo Chavez, for instance. Right now, you know, there are people who are political leaders who are closer to the -- Dr. Seselj's nationalist xenophobic than they are to the deliberative discourse that Europeans practice in their Parliaments. And I guess that's the main thing I want to tell you in answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mrs. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What happens when politicians issue threat messages to the public?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Well, the -- the findings of people in psychology, social psychology, and political psychology who studied the effects of -- of -- of discourse and -- and messages in the -- in the mass media on people's behaviours and beliefs and attitudes finds that the most important stimulus is a threat stimulus. And this will have a -- this will raise the fears of the -- of the audience. And if repeated enough, the people who listen to these messages will back action to remove the threat. Now, a threat can be moved by avoidance, but we're no longer in the age of hunters and gatherers where we can just go, you know, to the next valley. So in effect, what -- what a threat message produces is a -- a public willing to back political leaders and -- who use violent means, if necessary, or aggressive means, if necessary, to remove the threat. And in all the research on the impact of propaganda, the strongest stimulus has always been threat. Now, in this case, threat to the entire group or nation, rather than to an individual. And by the way, this threat doesn't necessarily have to be only physical threat. It could be demographic threat, like there is this other group and their numbers are increasing and our numbers are shrinking. It could be a cultural threat in the sense that we are losing our -- our traditions, our values, our way of life because we are assimilating to this -- to this other group. Or it could be economic threat; they are the ones who are successful and we are becoming impoverished. And, of course, it could be physical threat; they want to kill us or expulse us from our country. And usually it's a combination of all of these. And in fact in the case of the material that I've looked at, at one time or another Dr. Seselj really goes into all of these in some way.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now, before we review some of the records and examples of Mr. Seselj's speech, I want to ask you some questions about content analysis.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Well, I mean, content analysis has been done ever since there has been debate, as in -- in ancient Athens. What's -- what's new in content analysis is a more systematic quantitative content analysis that was developed really as a way of analysing propaganda in World War II. And when -- I actually studied content analysis with Bernard Berelson, who wrote the basic textbook on content analysis in the 19 -- late 1950s. At that time, there weren't any computers yet and the use of software to identify text with certain themes has been developed since that time, let's say, in the last 15 years or so. But what content analysis is you -- instead of just looking at text and picking out whatever suits you from somebody's discourse, a phrase here and a phrase there, and, you know, putting it together, what you do is you identify a large number of such texts on a particular theme and you actually analyse all of them by a uniform -- on a uniform code. You're looking always for the same things. And now, the code that I used is really at the bottom of every record, and it consists of really two items. I have identified themes from the nationalist literature and I've identified techniques from the propaganda analysis. Now -- and I've actually coded every one of the texts that we selected for both the themes and the technique. Of course, actually the -- the effect is produced by a combination of the theme with the -- with the technique. Now, the themes were, as I said, glorification of the -- of the in-group, negative labeling or stereotyping of the adversary, internal threats to Serbs, a threat being so important in all of this, as I've explained before. Dr. Seselj threatens others also in -- in many of these texts that I've looked at; advocates or expects violence; no compromise; omits nonviolence as a -- as a possibility to conflict management; external threats to Serbs. That's, again, the threats theme. Then expulsion, exchange of population; revenge retribution is another one. And denies responsibility or -- we call it plays the blame game. We didn't do it. They started it. It's not our fault, and so on. That's -- those are the themes that are in the nationalist literature, not just in Dr. Seselj's nationalist discourse. This is sort of standard nationalist discourse.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now, what do you mean by "persuasion techniques"?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Persuasion techniques are what I coded for next: Stereotyping and labeling is one. Generalisation; falsehood and misinformation. Again, threat discourse appears actually both in technique and in -- and in themes. Very important parts of -- the "Serbs threaten" discourse in Dr. Seselj, I broke out past atrocities committed against Serbs, which he mentions often. I thought that was an important thing to distinguish, break-out within the larger "Serbs threaten" category. And then victimhood. And these are known techniques of -- of really propaganda techniques, although we call them by the nicer word of "persuasion techniques." The only other one I didn't code for is repetition, because actually I was measuring repetition through doing the counts of how many times these negative stereotypes or the -- or the victimhood theme was -- was -- appeared in these -- in these texts.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: How did you select the records to review?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Well, we had these 40-some volumes available. Some of them --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Whose volumes? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Dr. Seselj's publications of his speeches, his appearances on television, I think issued by a publication house that his political party edited. It's not our compilation; it's his. It's his compilation. Certain volumes did not apply because they were not -- they didn't cover the 1991-1994 period. So we didn't look at them. Then instead of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- you just drew my attention to something. You're saying that you did not take a number of texts into account because they were not in the relevant period between 1991 and 1994; they didn't cover that period. Is that a deliberate choice that you made? Whereas, maybe in the texts that were not in this period, there would still be a logic. So why discard a period of time? Why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, actually, most of it starts in 1989/1990. And we actually included some from 1990. You know, that was my decision, although I was asked to do it for 1991-1994, because the indictment of Dr. Seselj covers the years 1991-1994, as far as I understand. Is that true, Madam Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Generally.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Yes. So that's what I did. I would also point out that we looked to see whether there were --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. The Prosecutor is misleading the witness by confirming his assumption that my indictment relates to 1991 to 1994. That's not true. My indictment covers the period of mid -- from mid-1991 until September 1993. And the expert witness must have laboured under that misconception all the time, and Ms -- Madam Prosecutor is only deepening that misconception.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, we considered the records from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: -- 1994 relevant to the extent they are describing or explaining Mr. Seselj's intentions or casting light on his motivations during the period covered by the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Following Mr. Seselj's words, you said, Mr. Witness, that you dealt with 1991 to 1994, and the indictment stops in September 1993. So you went a bit beyond that date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I started a little bit before that date and I went a little bit after that date. And that's just to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Fine. Well, this was the reason behind my question. I do not know what Mr. Seselj wrote in the 1980s or in the 1970s. I have no idea. But imagine that in the 1970s and the 1980s he wrote the same thing that he wrote in -- from 1991 to 1994, because there was a specific political situation that existed in -- in 1991 to 1994, the collapse of the former Yugoslavia. But if he had written the same thing beforehand, what would you have made of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what -- what he would have written about a hypothetical situation while he was in prison, I -- it doesn't make -- I don't fully understand what -- what that really means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, you said that he was in gaol. It's true that at one point of time Mr. Seselj was in gaol. But if before 1991 he dealt with -- he had dealt with Greater Serbia, Serbian people, history, the London Treaty, and so on, would that have changed your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, what -- whatever he wrote before the period that I looked at wouldn't make any difference to my conclusions whatsoever. I mean, he -- that's on -- what he wrote, what he thought during this period of -- of crisis and impending civil war and then war is what I looked at. It's on the record. What he thought of -- as a young man about some of these questions, I don't see -- he -- what we were looking at is not just Dr. Seselj's personal views, what he wrote in correspondence to his mother or said to his wife. What we looked at is the political discourse that he carried on at a time when he had a following. And he was a political leader. He founded a political party. He formed volunteers. When what he said was said over TV, over newspapers, in press conferences, and that is really what matters in this case and not what his personal, private views were before he had this political impact and audience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mrs. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: How many records did you review in total?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: We reviewed two sets. The first set was 240-some. And then we reviewed 180, I think, or something like that, 160. I don't have the exact -- I could look it up, but ... So --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you have a preset or predetermined figure in mind regarding the total number of records to review?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Not -- not really. As long as it covered these years and as long as we had sufficient instances from the television, radio, newspaper, and other media. And basically Dr. Seselj's discourse was very much the same during this time, and he said pretty much the same thing to -- in all these different settings, with -- you know, with variations. So I actually told the -- your -- your predecessor, who actually hired me to do this content analysis, that I didn't think there was any necessity to have some additional done after the first set of 240-some, but, you know -- but a lot of people feel uncomfortable with numbers. I don't, because I've done this repeatedly. And I said, "Okay, if you want to do it, I'll do it." But we found basically the same pattern of discourse. There was nothing unusual or different in the additional material that -- that I examined. So -- but since we've done it, we've put it into the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What happened when you found repetition in the messages you were coding in the records?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Well, we said, Enough is enough. How often do you want the same Seselj solution to the Albanian problem in Kosovo as he saw it, repeated over and over and over again, with -- with minor variations, he said pretty much the same thing. So instead of, you know, spending more time and spending more money of the -- of the Court's money, I said, you know, That's enough. We don't need it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Would repetition or the frequency of appearance of a particular threat add to or change your analysis?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: No. I mean, Dr. Seselj was using a -- one of the major techniques of propaganda is repetition; you keep repeating the same thing over and over and over and over again. And it does have, you know -- depending on whether there are other people who keep contradicting you, it does have an impact. It's a -- it's a well-known technique of -- of propaganda, and it -- and it works if there are no other contradictory messages in -- by, you know, other political leaders using the same media of communication. So basically that's what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me ask you to turn to your report.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Page 4.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: At the top of the page, you have a distribution by year. It's, for the record, 65 ter number 2797.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Mm-hm. Excuse me, we turned to what?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Page 4.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm understanding that people are also turning to that page. And it's page 4 in e-court in the English version. I wanted to ask you: Of the first group of records that you coded, what was the distribution by year?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Let me see. We have 1990, 12 per cent; 1991, 29 per cent; 1992, 20 per cent; 1993, 22 per cent; and 1994, 17 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I want to now turn to reviewing some of the records that you coded. And in the first category, I want to show an example from May 1991, and it's a video-clip. So we'll get that cued up. This is example number 31.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] The Serbian people in Serbia is above all endangered by this economic crisis, of course, which would not be cured. And the new Ustasha government in Croatia have again put the Kama knife under its throat. Should they attempt the new genocide against the Serbian people, we say to them again we shall take revenge for each Serbian life and we shall also ask to pay up for past crimes, also for crimes in recent history. And it is our duty to protect them, that it is primarily by their courage and their heroism that they show they are ready to sacrifice themselves for the defence of the Serbian land and Serbian borders to the great pride of all Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you may proceed, Mrs. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: When I show a video-clip, I will wait until the Bench looks up to ensure that I have allowed adequate time for the French interpretation. Thank you for letting me know.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: This is example number 31 from the second set of materials that you coded. Can you explain what you coded for this interview and why. It's 65 ter number 2875, with the evidence registry vision number 0602895.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Well, here you have several threat messages. And, of course, I -- "Serbs threaten" is what I quoted mostly. For -- like: "It is the obligation of all Serbs to help defend from the crazed Ustasha beast." This is not just a threat, but I also coded it as a negative label, or negative -- negative stereotype.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me interrupt -- let me interrupt for just a moment. This is e-court page number 49. I'm sorry. So the external threat that you were discussing, please continue.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Well, there are several mentions of threats. First, it says: "The Serbian people are existentially endangered. Then the new Ustasha leader and Tito General, Tudjman, has unsheathed an Ustasha Kama and put it under the Serbian people's throat." This is again a threat message. "Serbian men and women over there are trying to save their bare lives," and so on. So it's basically a very heavy dose of the threat message. I'd like to point out to the Court that even though dehumanisation is a category under "Persuasion techniques," I didn't -- whenever Dr. Seselj used such terminology as "the Croats are a poisoned snake" or "the Ustasha beasts," and so on, I didn't actually code it as "dehumanisation." Although, technically speaking, you could say, well, that's an example of dehumanisation if you compare negatively an entire people with a -- a beast, an animal, you know, especially a dangerous -- a dangerous -- a dangerous animal. But in my coding, I gave Dr. Seselj the benefit of the doubt. He has a very colourful way of speaking. He tends to be boisterous and do some exaggerations. And I decided that I would code those instances as negative stereotype, rather than dehumanisation. Because he used these phrases without going into a long paragraph of explaining, you know, and -- it's not like racist talk on the part of the Nazis or anything like that. But he uses these colourful little phrases, which compare the Croats and others to animals in a negative way. And I said, This is not really dehumanisation in the sense of the classic propaganda analysis of -- of, you know, Nazi Germany. So I just said, It's a negative stereotype. So in many ways, I was kind of erring on the side of giving Dr. Seselj the benefit of the doubt. You will also notice, if I can add this, that on several of the examples and records I actually coded nothing, because our search method produced text in which Dr. Seselj was talking about Serb/non-Serb relations. Well, if in that context he didn't use any, what I call, propaganda techniques and he didn't refer to "victimhood" or -- there wasn't any false information or misinformation in it, but it was, as Your Honour pointed out, just a kind of political discourse that you would expect a -- a politician to make in an adversary situation, then I coded nothing. So we -- we didn't just select the texts of Dr. Seselj that had propaganda content. Our method was to identify all the texts in which he talked on Serb/non-Serb relations, and then we coded them. And if there wasn't any propaganda content, I didn't code anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that we are at the point in time for the scheduled break. If I may bring that to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. We will now break for 20 minutes and resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have resumed our hearing. I would like to ask the Prosecution when it adduces a piece of evidence, when it's a video, to ask for the tendering into evidence of this document at the same time, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to mark for identification 65 ter exhibit number 2797, which is the expert report of Dr. Oberschall, including Appendix 2. I will move for admission of evidence at the conclusion of my direct examination with him. With that --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, when tendering any piece of evidence, the Prosecutor is duty-bound to explain what that piece of evidence means. We have seen a part of my interview, for instance, but the Prosecutor must say what it is about, when the interview was given, where, to whom. Without that, it cannot be tendered or admitted. Without all that, maybe we can assume that I told all that to my wife, sitting in my apartment. Everything that is tender must be completely clear, documented, and presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. For the time being, the Trial Chamber is seized of a request relating to the video, which is Exhibit number ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is exhibit number 65 ter 6015.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that is exhibit number 6015. This video, when is it dated? Do you have the date of the video or don't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: May 1991. It's a broadcast television programme entitled "Without a cut and an anaesthesia," by Studio TV NS. This is included in the description on our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me next mark for identification exhibit -- 65 ter exhibit number 7000, which is translation corrections to the appendix marked for identification as number 1. Next I want to mark for identification 65 ter exhibit number 2875, which is the addendum to Dr. Oberschall's report, in which he coded 156 additional examples. And last, I would move into evidence 65 ter exhibit number 6015, which is the video-clip played before the break, concerning example number 31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the video-clip number 6015 is admitted and the other documents you have mentioned are marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the video-clip with 65 ter number 6014 will be Exhibit P1. The video-clip with 65 ter number 6015 will be Exhibit number P2. The document with 65 ter number P02875 will be marked for identification as MFI P3. And document with 65 ter number 7000 will be marked for identification as MFI P4. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I thought I started with 65 ter exhibit number 2797, which is the expert report with its appendix.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI P5.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me turn to the answer to the Yugoslavian constitutional crisis proposed by Dr. Seselj. And I'm going to play a series of clips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To avoid objections, when there is a video-clip please give us a date, place, and origin.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: This is 65 ter exhibit number 6021. The date is July 25, 1991. And it is a television interview aired on TV Politika. This corresponds with example number 51.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Look, under Tito, Yugoslavia was an artificial state. It was a grotesque and imposed construct. It will never exist like that again. It could be like that only under the communist dictatorship. In actual conditions, those who are bigger and stronger will dominate. That is the way it is in the whole world. The next Yugoslavia is only possible under a Serb domination.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I would like to tender that for admission into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number P6.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to example number 51. It's Marked For Identification Exhibit 3, e-court page 78. Have you found the record? How did you code that utterance by Dr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Well, I -- I coded it under -- of course, it was "nations and nationalities" discourse. I mean, his theory of state formation and state and nation. I also coded it as generalisation -- sorry, "glorification of the in-group," when he says that "The next Yugoslavia is only possible under Serb domination." And he also says that the Serbs are the bigger and stronger and they will -- will dominate. And I think that's a -- a glorification of Serbs and Serbia. I also coded it as "generalisation." I think that was the most important part because he says "Yugoslavia was an artificial state. It was a grotesque and imposed construct" and "only possible under a communist dictatorship." Now, what he's referring to is the fact that Yugoslavia was composed of these different people. And there are many other examples in the world, actually, of perfectly viable states on all continents of what we call multinational or multi-ethnic states. There's Canada, in North America. There's Tanzania. There's South Africa, was actually -- became a -- a democratic state with a, you could say, even a more difficult, complex mixture of peoples and races than -- than Yugoslavia. Certainly India. Actually, I refer to studies that show that a -- a state that is composed of only one people or -- or nation with, you know, less than 10 per cent minority is actually the exception. There are very few of them. Japan is one of the -- one of the big ones. But actually most states are -- have substantial numbers of minorities or ethnic linguistic differences within them. So there's nothing artificial about them. At least, they don't think they're artificial. And this is part of Dr. Seselj's philosophy about the impossibility of bringing together into one state peoples of different culture, nationality, language, religion, and so on. And that's a -- I consider that a generalisation. I mean, a false generalisation, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let's now turn to example number 54, which is at e-court page 82. And I'm going to show video-clip C.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters need the 65 ter number for the video; otherwise, they can't interpret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please give the date of the video, the place, and so on and so forth, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is from the same television interview. It is part of P6. And the 65 ter number was 6021. And it's clip C within that group.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Dahl, from the interpreters. The demarcation between --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] [Previous translation continues] ... Live together in one state, provided that this state is democratic. And I believe that finally all the Serbs have come to realize that. As for our western borders, they stretch along the line Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Vitrovica, and I think there should be no concessions there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that clip into evidence. That's example number 54, clip C, from 65 ter number 6015.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P7.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: With regard to example number 54, Dr. Oberschall, how did you code this political discourse by Dr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Well, I coded it as "no compromise" because Dr. Seselj says: "As for our western borders, they stretch along the line between Karlobag, et cetera, Virovitica. And I think there should be no concessions there." And we're not talking about an internationally recognized border. We're not only talking about an internal border of Yugoslavia as it existed. We're talking about a border that Dr. Seselj is drawing in Croatia itself and he thinks there should be no concessions, that should be the western border of Serbia and -- and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now, let's go to example number 55. And we'll play -- which is at page 84 in e-court. And we'll play clip D of 65 ter number 6021.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Good evening. We have lost the line. Let us go back to what you said that we shall amputate Croatia. What does that mean? Seselj: That means once the army has withdrawn from Slovenia. You see, the Croats keep escalating the situation. Tudjman's throne is shaking. He has become nervous. They're going to make further wrong moves. They are making more and more mistakes, going from one mistake to another. They are now demanding that all the troops in the territory of today's Croatia should return to the barracks. Obviously, that cannot be allowed to happen. When the army withdraws from Slovenia, the troops should simply be ordered to withdraw from the territory of Zagreb, Rijeka, Istria, Kvarner, etc., up to the line Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Vitrovica does in effect amputate the Croats. It is much more convenient for us to have a border with friendly Italy, rather than with hostile Croatia. Italians in the Second World War frequently rescued Serb people from the Ustasha knife. Everybody knows that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I would move that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P8.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: How did you code example number 55?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Well, I coded it as "advocates or expects violence" on the basis of the statement: "This in effect amputates the Croats." Amputation is coercive, violent, bloody, painful, and it certainly conveys the image of a violent event, traumatic event.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let's move now to example number 56, which is at the next e-court page, 86. The video-clip is clip E from the same news programme at 65 ter exhibit number 6021.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] The news has been in circulation these days in Belgrade that Tudjman recently complained to the JNA generals that he had lost control over the situation in Slovenia. How can that be resolved then? Seselj: Well, of course he has lost control over all Serbian areas. The Serbian people cannot and will not ever recognize the Ustasha government. Tudjman's reign of terror. The Serbian people have liberated nearly all their areas. They have practically established a Serbian government there. A Serbian government has been established in Serbian Krajina. Serbs have their own government, their own ministries, army, police. Serbian government has been established in the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem too. Serbian government has been established there as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I would move the video-clip into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P9.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Turning to your coding sheet, for example number 56, how did you code that discourse?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Well, I coded it as an example of "external threat to Serbs," that's the reference to the Tudjman reign of terror and the Ustasha government. And then I coded it as "no compromise" again, like the last one, in the sense that -- the question is: How that can be resolved, then? Asked the interviewer. And Dr. Seselj says, Well, it's a fait accompli. You know, we've -- Serbs are in control of the Serbian Krajina and that's that, and the Croats have to accept it. So I coded that as "no compromise."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let's turn to example number 57 and clip F from 65 ter number 6021. It's another short segment from the same television programme.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] TV Politika. The Politika daily tomorrow will publish an interesting piece of news that a ship from Lebanon carrying 30 tonnes of weapons has been stopped at the town of Bar in Montenegro. For the time being, we don't know who these weapons were intended for. What is your comment? Seselj: The weapons are probably destined to Croatia. Croats are procuring weapons on all sides of the world. This embargo by the European Union is not effective enough. However, the Croats do not know how to use those weapons. That's they're main problem in the military sense. Militarily speaking, when armed Serbs show up, Croats run like a headless chicken. Even when they have a fantastic superiority in numbers, they are not able to win. TV Politika: "Such thinking is interesting for the simple reason that for many years or many decades we have lived with some completely different convictions, beliefs in brotherhood and unity. Seselj: "We lived under Communist indoctrination. We are liberating ourselves today and the Serbs have become aware of their strength again, of their former glory. Not a single Serb has fled from the battlefield of Slavonia and the Serbian Krajina in particular. You know when the battle starts, if there is someone fleeing, it is only Croats. That is the case everywhere. TV Politika: "You mean in these most recent events. Seselj: "In these events. TV Politika: "So you believe that there will be no large-scale conflict. Seselj: "There will be no large-scale conflict, but more blood will be shed. Blood will be shed. Many more victims will fall. There will be no war in the real sense of the word. Either if the army is able to counter those activities by the Croatian representatives in the federal government, if the army manages to keep its units and its weapons under control, then there will be no real civil war. Croats are not capable of entering into such a civil war."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I move that video-clip into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P10.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Looking at your coding sheet for example number 57, how did you code that political discourse by Dr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Well, there's, first of all, the glorification of the in-group, that is, the Serbs, who -- becoming aware of their strength of their former glory. You know, they're terrific fighters. None of them flees a battlefield, and so on. Then there's the negative labeling and stereotype of the -- of the Croats. They don't even know how to use weapons when they get them, and they're cowards. Then I also labeled it as, furthermore, as "stereotypes and labeling" in terms of techniques of persuasion, not only the theme or the content but as a -- as a way of talking about an entire people. It's not that some Croats are cowards and some don't know how to use weapons; they're all cowards; they're all obviously misfits. And then on -- I also coded it as "expects," in this case not advocates but "expects violence," because in the statement, although he says "there will be no large-scale conflict," he says "but more blood will be shed. Blood will be shed." Many more will fall. In other words, the course of action that he foresees and advocates will be bloody. And that's what this category stands for.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn to 65 ter exhibit number 6019, which corresponds with record number 210, which is one of the records attached to your first report. For the record, that's 65 ter number 02797, e-court page number 251. Turning now to the video. We'll play exhibit 65 ter number 6019. It is dated June 1, 1991. It's a television appearance with Mr. Seselj as the guest, with questions and answers, questions coming from the audience. It was broadcast on TV NS, the programme title "The other side of the face."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Vesna Radovanovic: How do you see Yugoslavia in the future and what is your attitude towards the peoples that comprise Serbia? I do not see any future for Yugoslavia. I think that there are two options in that regard. However, I am deeply convinced that in either case Yugoslavia will disappear. According to the first option, it is possible that Yugoslavia will fall apart into three states: Greater Serbia, small Slovenia, and an even smaller Croatia. According to the second option, should the Croats not like the first one, we the Serbs will reach an agreement with the Italians and in turn establish a Serb-Italian border along the Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Vitrovica line, as it is just to return to the Italians what is theirs. We can also talk to the Hungarians and Austrians as well. Austria would like to have access to the Adriatic Sea for Austria Germany and it would be right to afford Austria that. And especially with Hungarians because Hungarians have certain historical rights. There was a time when the Croats themselves handed over their state to the Hungarians who built a big port on the Adriatic coast in the last century called Rijeka. So perhaps it would be fair to return Rijeka to the Hungarians. It all depends on how these neighbouring states of ours behave. So far they haven't behaved well at all. You see the Austrians support our enemies. The Hungarians helped Croatia to arm itself. Their governments are short-sighted, not to use a worse expression. Serbs are their natural allies, if they want to attain certain objections. Hungarians will never be able to get a part of Vojvodina. That is something they've got to understand. The only territory they could get is in the West. Rijeka, which is beyond the Croatian Zagorje. Only Serbs can be serious allies in this case, and that is why the Austrians should think about their policy. If Hungarians and Austrians do not change their attitude, we will come to an agreement with Italy. Let them regret it later on."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Looking at your --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I move that into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P11.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Looking at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor, could you kindly wait for the interpretation in French to finish. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Looking at record number 210. Can you tell me how you coded Mr. Seselj's answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Well, as you will see, I actually did not code this as propaganda at all. The only thing I did is I -- the theme is nations/nationalities. And it's the kind of political discourse that the Presiding Judge was actually referring to, where there's negotiations between states in a peaceful way. There's no advocacy of violence or no mention of threat at all. And Dr. Seselj is in fact suggesting some pretty complicated but still, you know, diplomatic moves on international negotiations.
