And this is not -- this is his view. I happen to think it's kind of unrealistic, but there's nothing propagandistic about it. And some of the facts that he mentions there, like the Hungarians passing weapons to the Croats, was in fact -- did occur at this time. So it's not a misinformation at all. So I -- this is one of those items that we picked up in our search, and it was what I consider normal political discourse by political leaders.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let's turn to the next video-clip, clip B of 65 ter number 6019. That corresponds with record number 211, which is the next page in e-court. This clip is from the same Novi Sad Television programme.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] I still haven't answered the other question, how I see the peoples that comprise today's Serbia. Serbia today is comprised of the Serbian peoples, and national minorities also live in Serbia. In my opinion, they need to enjoy all civil rights and full freedom, full civil equality on the condition that they do nothing to bring into question the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Serbian state; that is to say, provided that they act as loyal citizens of the country in which they live. Those who bring into question the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Serb state, like the majority of Siptars do, will not have a place within the borders of present-day Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Dr. Oberschall, how -- I'm sorry. Let me first move the video-clip into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P12.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And, Dr. Oberschall, what do you make of Dr. Seselj's discourse that extends civil rights to citizens provided they are loyal to the country in which they live?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: I -- you have to understand one thing about propaganda talk, which we haven't had a chance to go into yet, but words don't have the same meaning that you and I would use in ordinary conversation or, in fact, is used in deliberative discourse. When you kill somebody, you say he committed suicide or he was shot while trying to escape. When you commit an aggression, it's called self-defence. If you're on a -- pretty much a dictatorial regime, you call it people's democracy. I mean, you use these words in a very different way in this kind of nationalist extreme discourse than -- than we do ordinarily, and -- than is the case in deliberative discourse. So when Dr. Seselj says: "Provided -- you know, people have all these rights provided they act as loyal citizens of the country in which they live," that makes a lot of sense if we interpret the word "loyal" as including the opportunity to form a peaceful political opposition, voice dissenting views, what is standard practice in -- in democratic states. But that is not the way he uses the word "loyal citizen." And the reason for that is the next line, which -- where he says: "Those who bring into question the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Serb state, like the majority of Siptars," meaning the Albanians in Kosovo, "will not have a place within the borders of present-day Serbia." Now, that I coded -- coded as a threat to the -- to the Kosovars -- I mean, the Albanians in Kosovo. And you have to understand that the context that the Albanian population was engaged in a general strike against the Serb authorities, who in fact had suspended their Assembly, taken away their political autonomy, and essentially were engaged in a non-violent opposition movement which we would consider the right of citizens in -- in any democratic country to -- to do. So that's the -- the context that -- where you have to sort of read this statement by Dr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let's turn now to record number 215, which is at e-court page 256. And the video-clip from the same television programme, clip D, at 65 ter number 6019.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] That was on the radio today at 3.00. I don't know if you heard that. How do you react to that decision? What do you say? Well, I personally, honestly speaking, can't wait for that Croat attack. It seems that the lesson of Borovo Selo was not sufficient. They need to get a much harder lesson. What about Bijeli Manastir? Has a Chetnik detachment already been formed in Bijeli Manastir? When will it be ready? Yes. Yes. There is also the Committee of the Serb Chetnik Movement and the Serb -- for Baranja. How do you -- Dusan Jandric from Futog has the following question: I will arrest Tudjman. That is what you say. And what kind of rifles are those that can hit the letter "U" at a 1.500-metre distance? I said that I would arrest Tudjman, Ante Markovic. I'm a wanted person in Croatia. That doesn't really bother me. I only move in Serbian lands, Serbian Slavonia, Baranja, Western Srem. Not in Croatia. Serb Chetniks today have very good rifles. In all fairness, they're very old, obsolete, manufactured in '42, but they've proven to be very efficient. You know when a Chetnik is a good marksman and when he hits a Croat in the forehead, then both of the Croats eyes pop out. Or if he hits him in the neck, then it cuts off his neck. These are very good rifles. Of course, we are only targeting those Croats who are attacking Serbian villages with weapons. We haven't targeted a single unarmed one until now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What -- what record are we referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'd like to move the video-clip into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number P13.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let's turn to record 215. That's at e-court 256.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: That corresponds with the video we just saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: How did you code that discourse by Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: I still don't know which record --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Record number 215.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: 215. I coded it as "advocates or expects violence and denies responsibility."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Let me just see. To the news that ... Well, he refers to the -- the Chetniks who have good guns and Thompsons manufactured in '42, shooting the heads off Croats with their eyes popping out, machine-guns that cut across people's neck. I mean, that's -- it's a very violent image, definitely advocates and expects violence. And then when he says, "We are only aiming for those Croats who -- with guns in hands attack Serb villages. We have not aimed for a single unarmed Croat," it means that he denies responsibility for any kind of an offensive -- everything's in self-defence. It's not our responsibility that there is this conflict. They started it. That's pretty standard discourse on denial of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let's turn now to 65 ter number 6014, which is a video-clip. And also let's turn to record number 112. That's at e-court page number 156.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And we'll play the video-clip. This is a speech from Mr. Seselj in April of 1991, and it's amateur photography.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] The new Ustasha chief and the Josip Broz's general Franjo Tudjman and the new Ustasha government in Croatia --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please play it from the beginning. You couldn't hear it right at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mrs. Dahl, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] The new Ustasha chief and Josip Broz's general Franjo Tudjman and the new Ustasha government in Croatia have again put the criminal Kama under the throat of the Serbian people. However, we will never allow a genocide to take place again. Should they attempt a new genocide against the Serbian people, we say to them that we shall take revenge for each Serb life and we shall also ask them to pay up for past crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Just a minute. We need to start from the beginning again. We need to hear what Mr. Seselj was saying during his discourse. Otherwise, we can't understand anything. So let's start again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Again, the criminal knife has been put under the throat of the Serb people, but we will never allow a new genocide to take place again. Should they attempt a new genocide against the Serbian people, we say to them: We shall take revenge for each Serb life and we shall also ask them to pay up for past crimes. Also for crimes in recent history. No deed will go unpunished, and we will not allow the consequences of the occupation over Serb lands and Serb people be sanctioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'd like to move that video-clip into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I ask the court officer to repeat the exhibit number with his microphone on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P14.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: The next clip is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Aren't you asking the witness to comment on the video and the classification, the coding?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I was going to put the two pieces together. But I'll ask Dr. Oberschall before we move away from this.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Based on what you heard of Dr. Seselj's speech, how do you classify his discourse there?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: This was not part of a record; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: It was just -- well, very definitely there was a strong threat to Serbs, just with the mention of genocide, past victimhood. Furthermore, there is a revenge and retribution discourse about how the Serbs should respond to -- you know, another renewal of this conflict. That's what I was able to -- to pick out just listening at -- without, you know, looking at it again. I might add that this is pretty standard discourse on the part of Dr. Seselj. This comes up again and again and again, in 1991, in 1992, in 1993, in -- on TV in all kinds of contexts. So it's -- it's almost predictable as to -- as to what he will say in these kinds of things. The past, the Serbs were victims, there was genocide. It's going to come again. The Croats are doing it. We didn't start it, and we have a right to take revenge and retribution against it. So this is very standard discourse.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now, based on your study of political sociology, is there other ways to remove a threat than through violent aggression?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Well, yes. And actually in one of the previous records, Dr. Seselj actually talked about diplomacy between states and negotiations with states. He does it seldom in the -- what we -- what we looked at, but it's not that -- first of all, he has a Ph.D. in -- in political science, so he obviously knows about this, that that's the usual way of dealing with interstate conflict and within states there are political ways of conflict management that do not involve violence and threats, and so on. So yes, I -- I say there very definitely are alternatives, and -- and in fact most states most of the time use those alternatives.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Well, let's look at another similar video. This is clip B from 65 ter exhibit number 6014.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Excuse me, exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: It's 6014. It's record number 112, I believe.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Or, I'm sorry, it's content similar to what you coded in record number 112, but I don't believe you coded this particular clip.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. As for the previous video-clip, the Prosecutor did not say where the speech had been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mrs. Dahl, this speech where I noted that Mr. Seselj was applauded at length by the people listening to the speech, where did this speech occur and when was it delivered?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: The speech was delivered in Jagodnjak in 1991, April. And now I'm going to play clip B from the same 65 ter number, which is been marked already as P1.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] The Croats, as far as we are concerned, can leave Yugoslavia as they please, whenever they want to, but we are openly letting them know that they will not take away a single foot of Serbian territory, not one piece of land where there are Serbian villages, destroyed Serbian churches, Serbian mass graves, Serbian camps, Serbian Jasenovacs. If we allowed that, we would be unworthy of our glorious ancestors and we would have to be ashamed in front of our descendants. The Croats can create their new state, but only west of the Karlobag-Ogulin-Karlovac-Vitrovica line. Everything east of that line is Serbian. We are not going to allow the Croats to manipulate the Bunjevci Serbs and the Sokci Serbs. They are Catholic Serbs who, we hope, will soon realize what kind of role the Vatican and the Ustasha leadership has in store for them against the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Based on what you heard from the video, how would you code that?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: I would like to point out to the Court that the so-called K-O-K-V line that Dr. Seselj advocates as the border between a Croatia as an independent state and the rest of Yugoslavia and the Greater Serbia, actually, leaves large numbers of Croats and other people on the Serb side of the border. In fact, in most of Slavonia there's a majority of -- of Croats and of -- of other non-Serb people. And drawing the line that he suggests would simply create large additional minorities on the Serb side of the border and in no way would resolve the question of majorities and minorities in this -- in this conflict. By re-drawing a line, you just create minorities where majorities existed and majorities where minorities existed. And moreover, the principle of drawing this line, as opposed to some other line, which in any case is not a negotiated line between two governments or, you know, sovereign political entities but depends on his particular preference for the boundaries of a Greater Serbia, I mean, is sort of no solution at all to the whole problem of how do you have people living together in one or two or several states in -- in a peaceful fashion. Sort of -- sort of -- that's sort of the basic thing that again and again comes up when Dr. Seselj proposes some kind of a resolution of the conflict between Croatia and Serbia by drawing lines and essentially not negotiating in a -- in a diplomatic or a political sense some kind of a re-thinking of what kind of a political structure to impose on these mixed region. It could be autonomous regions in a federation and there are many other constitutional ways of handling it. Canada did it in one way. The -- India does it some other way. And drawing just arbitrary boundaries based on force, essentially, to my mind is just no resolution at all of this whole question of multi-ethnic multinational states. And this again is very typical of -- Dr. Seselj talks again and again and again about this K-O-K-V line and the fact that he basically gives an ultimatum to the Croats, you either accept it or we will take it by force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I do have one thing to ask you, an additional detail. In this speech, Mr. Seselj is talking about this K-O-K-V line. It's not the first time he mentions it. He mentions it on several occasions. And this is his point of view, and he probably thinks that it would solve many problems. But this is not my question, but you draw conclusions which surprise me, because let's assume that this K-O-K-V line would be set up in the framework of an international agreement with international consensus. Then there would be Croatian minorities on the Serbian side. That's what you said. And you draw the conclusion that this would lead to problems. And while I was listening to you, I was thinking about a previous speech where he said that when there are minorities, these minorities are entitled to their rights. So when I connect these two speeches, when I combine them, I see no incoherence, but you draw different conclusions. Could you explain why, on the one hand, in one speech he's saying that when minorities exist, these minorities have the same rights as those who are in the majority. And if we assume that there is a Croatian minority because of the K-O-K-V line, your conclusion, the conclusion that you draw, is that this minority would be in an unfavourable situation. So why do you draw this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why do I draw the conclusion that -- if you start with a basically nationalist premise that there is one favoured nation in a state -- and, of course, the minorities have rights, but they do not really have the same political and cultural standing as the -- as the favoured nation. What you end up with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, you're saying minorities have rights, but you're drawing conclusions that they don't have the same political and cultural status. But why do you say that? You are making statements. These statements might be true, but you have to demonstrate that they're true. You're starting from the assumption that these minorities have rights, but you say, Yes, but they don't have the same political and cultural status. How can you draw this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you -- if you look at -- in my expert report, I actually have a whole section that deals with the question of states, nationalities, minority rights, and how sort of their different ways of dealing with these -- with these complicated questions in -- in states like Yugoslavia or India or Canada and -- and the like. Now, for the Yugoslav case, I cite an article written by a professor, Tibor Varadi, who is a law professor. He happens to be a Serb citizen. He also was the Minister of Justice, I think, in the first government after Communism in -- in Serbia. He just defended Serbia in an International Court here when it was being sued by Bosnia for reparations. And he wrote a very -- I thought a very deep and penetrating article about the kind of constitutional structure minority rights, group rights, and individual citizens' rights that would be appropriate to this kind of a complex situation, as is -- that -- you know, that we're considering now. So I don't know for how long I should really talk about this very complicated and involved topic, but I do refer in my expert report to the debate and also to a major Serb constitutional lawyer and the way he sees a resolution or the management of these kinds of conflicts through constitutional changes, boundary changes, and all I can say is that this kind of statement that Dr. Seselj makes about drawing arbitrary boundaries or shifting boundaries from one place to another, is simply not the way to go about doing this without getting into major trouble and conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, I'd like to turn to examples of Dr. Seselj's advocacy of expulsion and population exchange, because I think that answers your question regarding his solution for minorities in his newly-draw state lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Dr. Oberschall, if I may, let's -- may I ask you to turn to record number 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you get --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: I heard record number 3?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: This is page 57 in e-court. And for the record, this is an extract from Dr. Seselj's book, Volume 17, entitled "Destruction of the Serbian national identity." He reprints an interview with Dragan Ciric [phoen] and the date attributed by Dr. Seselj is April 15, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In the context, Dr. Oberschall, of the Albanian question, so to speak, what does Dr. Seselj propose to do with people he considers minorities within the Greater Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Well, in this case, we're talking about the Albanians in Kosovo and --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Judges, why would the Albanian issue be relevant to my indictment? I have a completely different discourse on Albanians than I have towards Croats and Muslims. And I am not indicted for Albanians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mrs. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, Dr. Seselj's advocacy is population exchange, and it's directed at Croats, Bosniaks, Albanians, anyone who is left inside a border that he draws and whom is not -- who does not consider himself to be an enlightened Serb or an awakened Serb. I will demonstrate by going through a number of written examples that Dr. Seselj's discourse consistently calls for expulsion of minority ethnic groups, and even majority ethnic groups to make room for ethnic Serbs he thinks should live within the borders of a Greater Serbia. Then we will discuss what he considers to be a civilised population exchange, which is his euphemism for ethnic cleansing. So I'd like to put the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: -- back to Dr. Oberschall.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What does Dr. Seselj suggest should be done with people once the border is re-drawn?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Well, in -- in this particular case, in record number 3, he suggests that a belt of about 50 kilometres along the Albanian border, all the Albanian population has to be moved -- moved out or into other parts of Yugoslavia. He says they should get monetary compensation. This most fertile land, he says should be given to the -- to the army and that it should be settled, systematically inhabited by a Slavic population and that all 360.000 Albanian -- he calls them emigrants, but they're actually inhabitants, who moved from Albania to Yugoslavia from April 6, 1941 to the -- to this date -- that's actually a fictitious number that's not substantiated by any historical records -- as well as members of their families be handed over to the UN High Committee -- I guess he means high commissioner for refugees, since there are so many rich, specious and under-populated countries that can be -- that can take them and prove their -- and prove their humanity. That is -- well, it's -- he's very sarcastic here, but he essentially wants to get rid of the Albanians and have them settle wherever they can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, I allowed you to answer the question, despite the objection raised by Mr. Seselj, for the following reason: In your report, I did read about this question of the 360.000 Albanians who supposedly -- who came to Kosovo, and you're contesting, you're challenging this. You are saying that the figure is not right. Well, while I was reading your report, I was wondering what you were basing all this on. Why do you say that 360.000 Albanians did not emigrate from -- starting in the 1940s, emigrate to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this -- you know, this -- this figure is used by Serb nationalists, and so on, but the -- the standard history of Kosovo written by Noel Malcolm and also by Tim Judah is what I quote to challenge this figure. And if you will look at the actual --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what are the official figures, please? What would they be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The official figures, I -- I would have to look at what I had written. I mean, I don't remember all these -- these figures, but they're -- they're very small. They are -- they are -- they're in the few thousands, certainly not in the 360.000. But if you would like to, I can check to see what the actual historians of this period say about these figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm listening to you. But if this figure is so controversial and if I refer to the traditional example, you know, between Mexico and the United States, where Mexicans cross the border every day to go to the United States, did you envisage the possibility that as of the 1940s there might have been migration flows for different reasons, for political, economic, or social reasons which -- and because of that -- and it wouldn't be just a few thousands that would have emigrated but hundreds of thousands.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, Noel Malcolm and Tim Judah look at all the estimates, all the figures, all the population flows, and they come to certain conclusions. And I'm not going to dispute that. I'm not an -- an expert on the demography of Kosovo in the 1940s, so I rely on those who are. My -- I could say another thing about numbers, Your Honour, if I may. The -- a part of propaganda is actually to inflate or deflate figures by, you know, not a factor of 2 but sometimes a factor of 10 or even more. Now, for instance, Dr. Seselj uses certain figures about the Ustasha killings of Serbs in World War II and how many Serbs died in the various camps, and so on. And what I'm doing is I'm quoting the actual researchers and the historians who looked at those figures and I provide the best figures that these objective researchers have looked at, and they are much lower than the -- the victims claimed by Dr. Seselj and in fact other Serb nationalists. I would also like to point out that in his testimony for -- on the -- in the Milosevic trial, Doctor -- Dr. Seselj himself said that he uses figures for propaganda purposes. He went around claiming, I believe it was 30.000 volunteers that he -- that he organised. And under -- testifying under oath at the Milosevic trial he said that that was only 10.000, as a more accurate number. And I think when the Prosecutor, Dr. Nice, asked him about this discrepancy, Dr. Seselj said, Well, you know, we're politicians. We use figures. Whatever suits us. It's part of our profession to make propaganda and to give -- and to actually tell lies. So my approach to Dr. Seselj's figures --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- to be very cautious --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Objection raised by Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, it is completely inappropriate for the expert witness to interpret off the cuff my alleged testimony in the Milosevic trial. In order for him to be able to interpret that, the expert witness would have to have the proper quotation in front of him, rather than making things up and saying what he believes that I said at that time, because I certainly didn't say it the way the witness is representing it. It is inappropriate for an expert witness. It is perhaps excusable if we are talking about a half-literate ordinary witness, a villager from God knows where. But an expert witness should give an appropriate quotation from such-and-such a trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Seselj raised an objection, but I was going to ask you the same question, a similar nature. You said that you looked at the answers given in the Milosevic case by Mr. Seselj. Did you do this out of intellectual curiosity? Because this was not exactly what you had been asked to do. So why did you check what had been said in the Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I actually checked to see what was going on at this Tribunal not just in the Milosevic case but in a number of other cases. For instance, General Galic's trial, a lot of the Prijedor prosecutions, and some of the others. I mean, it's very important for me to keep abreast of, you know, new information that this Court is producing just on a weekly basis on the events and the -- and the people and the organisations that I -- I write about and that I -- I have to know about in order to be an expert. So I have the quotes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood you well. Thank you. But are you absolutely sure of the words spoken? Because obviously there is -- the words spoken are challenged here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have actually written them down. And I have them in front of me here. Mr. Nice -- let me see. Dr. Seselj was a witness on behalf of his former rival, President Milosevic, and he was asked by the Prosecutor Mr. Nice about incriminating statements he had made against Milosevic in the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. Oberschall should say from which page he's reading. I suppose that's his addendum report that I received a few days ago, two or three days ago. That's where you mentioned it. You must tell me which page it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Page 4 of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have the reference, please? Do you have the reference of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges can always check anyway.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. It's -- it's -- it's page 4 of my addendum, but the number printed by the court is 06148632.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: The 65 ter number is 7001. And it's at the back of the appendix. And I will give you the e-court number in a minute, if you'd like. Page 4. Mr. Seselj's testimony in the Milosevic case has been admitted in this case as an exhibit. It hasn't been assigned a number, however, but it's in a prior Trial Chamber session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We have the text on screen and we see in English: "[In English] Yes, political discourse is full of lies."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, my objection related to the specific quotation by Mr. Oberschall, just one sentence that he tried to interpret is correct, that in propaganda -- for propaganda purposes I claimed there were 30.000 volunteers, but the real number was in fact closer to 10.000. Everything that Mr. Oberschall added to that is an arbitrary fabrication. In order to prove it now, he refers to other parts of the transcript. The two were not directly related. In the specific case, speaking of the number of volunteers, it is recorded in the transcript what I said exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Your objection has been noted down and the Judges will sort all this out. Now, we'll continue. So, Mrs. Dahl, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: The court officer has indicated that we're taking a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. It's 12.20, and we'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. And before giving the floor to Mrs. Dahl, I have an information -- a logistic information. Tomorrow the Milosevic Chamber will render judgement at 9.00 a.m. in this courtroom. We will have, therefore, to move to Courtroom II, and after the first break, we will come back to Courtroom I. So, Mr. Seselj, tomorrow at 9.00 we will first sit in Courtroom II, and at 10.30 we'll move back to courtroom -- Courtroom I, because room -- Courtroom I is going to be occupied by the Milosevic judgement. Mrs. Dahl, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Just before the break, Mr. Seselj raised an objection to a quotation Dr. Oberschall had in his report from Mr. Seselj's testimony in the Milosevic case. I want the record in this case to be absolutely clear and, to the best of my ability, free from any incorrect statements. I found the quote that Dr. Oberschall referred to from Mr. Seselj's testimony on 7 September 2005, pages 4323, line 23 -- excuse me, 43923, line 23 to 43925, line 3. Question from Mr. Nice: "The next question is a very simple one,

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And was it your intention at the time to say something that was untrue; yes? Answer from Mr. Seselj: "Yes. Within the propaganda efforts of the SRS against the authorities of Mr. Milosevic and him personally, this is the mildest kind of thing I said then. There are things that are far more vigorous than that. Question: "It was a lie? Answer: "No, Mr. Nice. If you were an educated person, then you would have read Hannah Arendt's book "Truth and Lies in Politics." Oh, fine. So that's the best thing to do, to turn off the witness's microphone because you don't like the answer."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'd like now to return to Dr. Seselj's theme of expulsion and ethnic cleansing in his political discourse. First I'd like to tender for identification 65 ter exhibit number 7001, in which a portion of the Milosevic transcript is quoted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Judges, Ms. Dahl just confirmed what I objected to in relation to what Mr. Oberschall was saying. What I uttered in the Slobodan Milosevic trial - and I was interrupted, because that Trial Chamber did not like my answer - has nothing to do with my cited statement about the number of volunteers of the Serb Radical Party. In one context, my statement cannot artificially be grafted onto another one. Every statement is made in a particular context. The main thesis is that if there is political squabbling and when you say something that you know is not true, and everybody else knows it's not true, then you're trying to challenge, hurt, provoke, insult, and so on. But you do not have a feeling that you're saying an untruth and other people do not take it as an untruth. It can be a witticism, it can be a political provocation, but I am supposed to teach the ABCs of politics here to Mr. Oberschall and Ms. Dahl. I think that doesn't make sense. Mr. Oberschall should provide information accurately and precisely. That's the only thing I'm asking for. It is not for him to try to remember things based on his own memory that are wrong at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, Mrs. Dahl quoted an answer you made to Mr. Nice, and you said earlier that the Chamber had cut off your microphone at the time. So you're telling me that the answer you gave was not complete? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, certainly it was not complete, like many other answers, but it doesn't really matter in this case, because so far I did not see you switching off my microphone, so you're not selecting my answers according to a nonjudicial criterion. And that's what happened then. Whenever I was saying something that they didn't like, they would switch off my microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. My position is very simple: I do not see why I would shut off your microphone. As long, of course, as this -- everything you say is within what is allowed in the controversial -- adversarial procedure. So we will see -- we will see later on whether this quote should be in the record or not, given what has been said. Mrs. Dahl, you can resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Seselj's status as a self-represented accused gives him the opportunity to speak, particularly in making objections, which is, of course, perfectly consistent with his status of representing himself. I would like, however, the Court to warn him that what he says will be used by the Prosecution against him. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you've said this -- you've said this over and over again. He knows this very well. He knows that everything he is saying can be used. He knows this.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm -- the length of his speaking objections add to the evidence that we will argue at the close of the case. Now I'd like to mark for identification 65 ter exhibit number 7001.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours that, will be MFI P15.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to 65 ter number 6011. It's a video-clip from Croatian TV reporting Mr. Seselj's activities at a press conference.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And the format is called picture-on-picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What's the date, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: My record here indicates 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Again, Seselj asked to speak, the briefest gist of his discussion, this time could be described as a suggestion that if the Croats were expelling Serbs from Zagreb then what were the Croats waiting for in Belgrade? According to him, this represents a retaliation. Mahmut Memic and Antun Skenderovic reacted to that saying the Seselj's viewpoints have already been known but this could -- that this time he said it from the Assembly floor and thus marked the Croats in Serbia as hostages. Further in his report, Seselj maintained that this regime was too lenient towards Croats and that after this, all the Croats will be expelled and that those who live in Serbia will not sleep peacefully until they are moved out. By the same right Tudjman used to expel Serbs, we will expel Croats, said Seselj. Adding that he wanted to disperse another illusion about the loyal behaviour of Croats in Serbia since he maintained they were aiding the Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreters drew the attention of the Judges on two -- on two problems. The English text, which is sometimes -- has been given, does not really reflect what was said by Mr. Seselj. And also because Mr. Seselj speaks extremely fast, it's very hard to translate the videos. Maybe if it's very important, we need to replay this sequence in order to correct whatever may be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me replay the sequence and let me correct my description of it, because it is actually clip G in my exhibit list that I've given out. There is also a transcript from the Serbian Parliament session of Mr. Seselj. The correct date is April 1, 1992. And I apologise for the confusion. So why don't we at this point replay the video-clip.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that the speech is too fast to render itself for interpretation in the courtroom and it is not even directly Mr. Seselj's speech. It is a journalist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... We have to play it again, because we did not get a translation. It was too fast and we don't know what Mr. Seselj exactly told to Parliament. So please play it again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Seselj asked for the floor again and this time his -- the briefest gist of his discussion could be the following suggestion: What were the Croats waiting for in Serbia? Looking at what happened in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Note: The speaker is too fast for proper interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Separately, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Separately, Your Honour, we will file a detailed transcript that slows down the speech so that it can be properly assessed by the Chamber. I'm sorry for the speed at which these videos are played. We move --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree that the detailed transcript should be admitted into evidence, but I am against having this footage admitted, because these are not my words. These are a journalist's interpretation. Ms. Dahl said that this was from Croatian TV from a Croatian TV show "Slikom na Sliku"; however, I hear that this is a Serbian journalist speaking ekavian. They could have obtained this from Belgrade television or from the national parliament. They could have gotten the original. Journalist's interpretations cannot be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Seemingly we have two issues here. One is what the journalist is saying; and two, the words spoken by Mr. Seselj in parliament. What you are interested in are the words of Mr. Seselj, not the journalist. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In part, Your Honour, I agree with that. There are two issues here: One is what Mr. Seselj said; and the second is what effect it had or what was understood by the audience, what it motivated people to do. And I will present the transcripts of the television programme as well as the transcript from the Serbian Parliament session so that there is a complete record and no question of misunderstanding. I'd like at this point, however, to move into evidence 65 ter number 6011, clip G.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has decided to give an MFI number, pending the translation. So, Registrar, could we have an MFI number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, MFI P16.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Dr. Oberschall, were you able to listen to the broadcast of Mr. Seselj's speech with sufficient detail to comment on what categories it falls in?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Well, it definitely falls into the expulsion/exchange of population category.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you to turn to -- [FRENCH INTERPRETATION ON THE ENGLISH CHANNEL]?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj. [FRENCH INTERPRETATION ON THE ENGLISH CHANNEL].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... In a position to characterise the journalist's interpretation and to speak about me. This is not a question of my words verbatim. When he is an expert witness at a trial for this journalist, then he can make such comments. Now he is giving his comments regarding the journalist, believing that he is making a comment with regard to me. Ms. Dahl should have brought him the stenogramme, the stenographic notes, not somebody else's speeches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, in the video-clip we have just heard, we could hear the journalist and we could hear Mr. Seselj, as well as an MP who takes the floor. So please only comment on Mr. Seselj's words, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can repeat my question. It was whether he could hear --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: -- the official's speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So please repeat your question. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, not a single one of my words is here. You can only see my picture here. I was 16 years younger then, and that's the only thing you can establish. It is only the journalist who's speaking there. There is not a single live word from me there. The expert cannot give his comments on that. He has to have the stenographic notes put to him, and then he can comment on that, unless he's already dealt with it through some of my books and put that into his expert report. He cannot characterise a journalist's interpretation as my own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... Just a minute, Mr. Seselj. The way I understood things: When one can see you speaking, the translation is a translation of your own words. And now you're telling us that we have heard the translation of what the journalist has said. Mrs. Dahl, what are we to make of this, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I have to say that there are so many examples of Mr. Seselj calling for the expulsion of Croats, calling for the exchange of populations, that to quibble about this really is a waste of time. I can bring the parliamentary transcript if Mr. Seselj is at this point walking away from his own words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Dahl, I think there are two issues here. We see Mr. Seselj taking the floor in parliament in Belgrade, and Mr. Seselj is saying that on the tape he cannot hear his own words, so -- which is a problem. So what did he actually say? We all have a translation of what has been said about Serbs and Croats. You talk about expulsion. I did not hear the word "expulsion." I heard that the Serbs were going to live in flats that belong to Croats, and vice versa. So that's how things stand. This is a hearing before a criminal court. You need to be extremely concise and weigh your words, because this can have consequences, and you cannot attribute to Mr. Seselj on the basis of this video-clip what you wish to attribute to him. So please give us a video which spells this out more clearly, because we do not have those words spoken by Mr. Seselj. It seems like we have the comments here of a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm in agreement that words matter particularly in this case. I appreciate that we have this video marked for identification, and I have offered and will provide a detailed transcript that allows proper interpretation, as well as the transcript from the Serbian Parliament session in question. I think the news broadcast itself does have relevance to this case. Dr. Oberschall's expert analysis is the use of mass media and Mr. Seselj's persuasion techniques. The news coverage that he had saturated the region with his brand of political discourse, and so I believe that there are two aspects of this video that make it relevant, not just what Mr. Seselj said but what was understood by people reporting on what he said. I will leave that exhibit marked for identification and supplement the record so that you have the information that you need to make a decision on it. I would like to turn now to example number 84. This is a record in the Exhibit Marked for Identification P3. You can find it in e-court searching record 65 ter number 02875. It appears at page 128.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: This is published in Politika, April 4, 1992. Dr. Oberschall, would you review the record and your coding and please read out the portions that you found significant regarding Mr. Seselj's discourse.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Could you give me the record number again.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: It's example number 84, which would be for you in your binder printed page number 127 of your addendum.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Example 84?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Okay. And I should read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yeah, please familiarise yourself with it, and then we can discuss what you coded and why.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Well, the -- the way I coded it is, again, the topic is the "expulsion and exchange of population" and, furthermore, there's a threat to Serbs. In other words, the threat is Tudjman expelled several thousand Serbs from Croatia, and we have to expel all Croats from Serbia. The Croats have no business staying in Serbia. So that involves both a threat and also what Dr. Seselj refers to as "the exchange of population." But as you say here, it really means "expel." I mean, he says that, "expel all Croats from Serbia. The Croats have no business staying in Serbia." And moreover, he looks at them as kind of a fifth column who will be disloyal to the state and help the adversary in some fashion, but there's no real evidence on this particular point. So that's how I coded it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Does the record indicate how Mr. Seselj proposed people should be removed? And let me give you a moment to read it.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: It says that "We will simply put them on buses and escort them to the border."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In your review of Mr. Seselj's discourse on population exchange, did you find a large number of records on that issue?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you describe --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: -- their characteristic.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Well, the characteristic is what I refer to as a euphemistic language about voluntary or population exchange, is how he routinely refers to it. But in -- in propaganda language, that generally means that it's coercive. You force people out against their will, whether they like it or not. You make no distinction about what they did and who they are, as long as they belong to a certain category. And essentially you ask them to pack a suitcase, put them on a bus, and you dump them at the border. And that's supposed to be, you know, a voluntary population exchange. I mean, I -- I can only say it's not the right word to describe what is happening on the ground to people when they are treated this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Based on your research in the former --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: -- Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge. Objection. Before the next question, I ask you to order the expert to throw that chewing gum out of his mouth, because in this way he is offending the Trial Chamber and me too. He is still chewing his gum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the witness is answering a question. You might not like his answer and it could be questioned, but please listen to what he's saying. And tomorrow during your cross-examination you can put questions. And hopefully this will reveal the truth. But for the time being, we are just at the initial stages of a process and we are talking about exchanges and expulsion. You are giving us your view, and we shall see what we make of this. So please proceed, Mrs. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me return to the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, may I say something else? May I say something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I like Mr. Oberschall's answers very much. I have been nodding to everything that he's said until now today, as if he came as a Defence expert, but I don't think it is appropriate for him to go on chewing his gum. If you think it is appropriate, then I'm not going to object to that being done by any witness ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, expert witness, I didn't know that you had chewing gum in your mouth. Now, you've done away with that. That's fine. Please proceed, Mrs. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention to the phrase from Mr. Seselj saying that - and I'm back at example number 84 - "They are saying that the expelling of the Croats would not be a democratic solution; however, that method has already been applied in the world and it proved to be good in the situation where people cannot live together." Can you help analyse the content of those two sentences.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Certainly. There's a standard historian volume on population exchanges, population expulsions, ethnic cleansing, and the historian's name is Najmark and the book's title is "Fires of hatred." Actually, I refer to it. And it has really the best documentation on what actually happens when there are exchanges of population, expulsions of population, whatever you want to call them. Now, at various times Dr. Seselj gives examples of what he considers voluntary exchanges of population that took place and resolved questions of minority/majority conflict, one that he likes to cite is the India-Pakistan break-up and the -- you know, creating a border between India and -- and Pakistan, and so on. And if you actually look at the historical record, this was one of the greatest mass tragedies in twentieth century history. There was about more than a million people were expulsed or fled from what is now India to what is now Pakistan and there was also a flow in the opposite direction. A lot of these people were killed or starved during this transit. They practically took only what they could carry on themselves. And it definitely is looked upon by the Indians and the Pakistanis as -- and, of course, everybody else, as a great -- as a great tragedy. There's another example that he cites in a critique of my content analysis, his 156-page rejoinder to me, he cites the Greek-Turkish population -- he calls them exchanges, but they're actually expulsions and ethnic cleansing at the end of the Greco-Turkish War in 1922/1923. And I actually went back to Najmark to look at actually, you know, what happened and his descriptions of it, which I do give in my addendum of about 15 pages. I actually quote what Professor Najmark writes about this so-called voluntary population exchange, which, again, ended up in a -- a great tragedy, deaths, starvations, and -- and very difficult relocation experience of the people who survived all these population exchanges. If you look at the Najmark book, which starts with the Armenians and the Turks, then the Greeks and the Turks, the -- and goes through World War I and all the population expulsions and ethnic cleansing after the Versailles Treaty, through the World War II and the aftermath of World War II, plus the Stalinist expulsions of people from their customary territory in the Soviet Union, and so on, down to the -- the present, the Yugoslav situation, you will find out that no matter what somebody calls it and what beautiful title you give, what it amounts to is a lot of people are forcefully removed from their homes, quite a few of them die during this process. They are deprived of their property. They end up as refugees, permanent refugees in some other country. And pretty much that's the story of twentieth century population exchanges. There is no single example, unless it's on a very small, limited scale and a very small -- and a very small district, of major population exchanges in -- in twentieth century history. This is European history, but it's true also for other parts of the world.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Would you consider that Mr. Seselj's characterisation of historical population exchanges is accurate, then?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: No, of course not.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to a record you coded concerning what Mr. Seselj thought about the exchange of population between India and Pakistan. I'm referring to Prosecution Exhibit Marked for Identification 5, e-court page number 231 in English, 247 in B/C/S. And, I'm sorry, Dr. Oberschall, for all of these numbers. For yours --

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: -- it's record number 192.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Record 192.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'd like to read this into the record. This was re-published by Mr. Seselj himself in Volume 22 of his publication called "Television battles." The document date is 8 April 1992, and it was an interview at the television station Studio B. Mr. Seselj reprints himself as having said, secondly, as Mr. Lilic has said: "Yes, there are some good Croats. I could agree with him in principle. There are probably some good ones somewhere, but I have never met one in my life. So I don't know where those are. It was made clear to us that those who act the best, who look the best to us, are in fact the most dangerous. They are our worst enemies. They are the greatest criminals, like, for example, Ante Markovic. You know how heartily Serbia welcomed Ante Markovic, how much it supported him and how hard it was to get rid of him once it became clear that he did much more damage than Tudjman. Tudjman is an outspoken Ustasha, and he was useful to the Serbs. He awoke the Serb national consciousness and united the Serbs in the Croat federal unit." I'm skipping ahead: "But those that pretend that they are good, that they are our friends, they always bring the worst destruction upon us, starting from Tito onwards. "Concerning the question of exile of the Croats from Serbia, I believe that it is not contradicting any of the elementary democratic rights. Because if we look at the international experiences in that respect, we shall see that there is nothing new in this idea. The Germans were expelled from Poland; the Germans were expelled from Czechoslovakia, from the area of the Sudet. The Germans were expelled from Yugoslavia. Why not the Croats then? If this is now a crime against the Croats, then it had also been a crime against the Germans. Either we will expel the Croats now or bring back those Germans. A dilemma of principle is posed here. After all, there was an exchange of populations during a demarcation between India and Pakistan. It happens in other places in the world as well. Why? If so much hate appears between two peoples that it renders their normal cohabitation possible [sic], if a life together is impossible (which is so obvious in this case) then the populations should be nicely exchanged. And what does that mean? It is unbearable to the Serbs to live in Croatia, but Croats can live in Serbia? Why and for what? And where are those 200 to 300 thousand Serbs going to go when they arrive from Croatia? Those that stay on the territory of the Serb Krajina and that will potentially inhabit here, but the accommodation capacity of the area is limited. The rest shall come to this shrunken Serbia. Where to put them? Where will they live? Where will they work? We cannot. Serbia has no money to build houses for them, to build buildings, to employ them, and so on. The most elegant solution: Nicely to -- Croats to Croatia, Serbs to Serbia. Every bird to its own flock. And let it be settled forever. Why would we leave here someone who is going to destabilise us constantly, who is openly cooperating with Ustashas and their actions, like when those Ustasha were transported to the Hungarian border. After all, do not forget that a significant number of today's Croats in Serbia were sent here by Pavelic during the Second World War to the area of Srem and especially in the area of Slankamen; they are the worst Ustasha from Western Herzegovina. And how many Ustasha are in the municipality of Zemun? What to do with them?" How did you code that, Dr. Oberschall?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Well, there was a lot there. And, of course, it's mainly about the expulsion and exchange of population, but it's -- he's also stereotyping the Croats here, essentially saying they're all the same and even the good ones are dangerous, things of this nature, which are negative stereotypes. He's also talking about an internal threat to the Serbs if these Croats were to remain in -- in Serbia. Of course, he gives a lot of reasons why he advocates this, what he calls, the exchange of population. And maybe I can talk to that point --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: -- a little. First I would like to say I see a contradiction here. On the one hand, we've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You remember a previous record where Dr. Seselj says that as long as citizens are loyal, they will have the same human rights, citizen rights. And now he says here that even the good Croats should really not stay in Serbia, because in fact they're the most dangerous, which I -- it really is -- it's a total contradiction to me. Secondly, he -- he maintains -- you know, he gives reasons that amount to saying that just because people can -- perpetrated horrors and atrocities and ethnic cleansing in the past and in recent European history, it's okay to do the same thing, which is a total non sequitur as far as I'm concerned. I would never plead not guilty killing somebody by saying other people are -- have also, you know, committed murder. A housing shortage? I mean, that's not a reason for kicking out an entire -- you know, the Croats from Serbia. And he gives these other sort of reasons. I -- I would also like to point out something important. He keeps maintaining that Serbs and Croats had been "hating each other" from time immemorial or for a long time and therefore they would never be able to live together in a -- in a peaceful way and manage their conflicts in a -- in a -- a non-violent manner. I've actually looked at the history of Serb-Croat relations, and I have a whole section from a history book that actually Dr. Seselj quotes from a lot, John Lampe. And I've taken something like half a dozen concrete examples in the history of the -- of that region where the -- the Serbs and the Croats actually cooperated militarily, politically, culturally, and in substantial numbers, not just as a -- as a peculiarity or as an idiosyncratic incident. I would also like to point out to the Court that after the Dayton Peace Treaty there -- there was a settlement between Serbia and Croatia on what was going to happen to Vukovar, Osijek, and essentially Eastern Slavonia. Eastern Slavonia was going back from Serb military occupation to -- to be part of Croatia. But in this agreement -- it was an international treaty backed by the European Union and the NATO military. It was made very clear that there was not going to be -- that NATO and the European Union was not going to stand for any kind of an ethnic cleansing by the Croats of the Serbs who were in Vukovar at the end of the war and that the Croats who were coming back were going to be able to recover their homes and properties or, you know, get some compensation for them. And what in fact happened since 1997 is that at first a small number, but then a substantial number of the Croats who had been expelled or fled from Vukovar during the war have actually gone back, and the Serbs who were there during the war have stayed. And there was a major study done by the University of California by the law faculty and anthropology in 2001, I believe, and a major book was written about this experience of the Croats coming back and living together with the Serbs in Vukovar, which was, as you well know, the site of the most horrible war and civilian casualties, and so on. And I'm not saying that the findings are that people are embracing each other in the street, and so on, but they have worked out, the Croats and the Serbs, these people who allegedly have been hating each other all the time and have just recently killed each other, they are living in Vukovar. Vukovar is being rebuilt. It's a functioning community. There's municipal government and services that both the Croats and the Serbs participate in and enjoy. And it's just another example that the kind of conceptions and political philosophy of Dr. Seselj, plus his use of history in a -- really a mistaken way -- and I give him -- and, you know, he's an -- he's an educated person. He should know what happened between India and Pakistan when there was a partition. I mean, it's common knowledge. It's in the history books everywhere. Well, in any case, what -- this particular record -- and I apologise for speaking for so long -- does indicate that the solution tried in many countries -- and I'm not saying that there are no problems between ethnic groups and religious groups and no conflicts exist, but in many countries these things are worked out politically, culturally, and -- and they -- and they work. And his conception that it doesn't work and therefore you have to kick people out from one place to another, draw borders, and so on, is -- is -- simply does not agree with what we know in social science and in history.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now to record number 191. This is e-court page number, in English, 230; B/C/S page number 246. And in the interests of time, let me publish what's in this record. This is an interview republished by Mr. Seselj. The date of the interview is May 7, 1993. It was published in Mr. Seselj's collective works, Volume 28, "Current political challenges."

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Interviewer: "According to the plans, the Serbs in Bosnia are entitled to 43 per cent of territories, and they won over 70 per cent. They have to return a portion of the territories. Seselj: "Nothing will be returned here, because the Serb refugees from that area -- from the area that is now controlled by Croats and Muslims inhabited those areas. Zvornik is now filled with Serbs. At one time, many Muslims used to live there. There has been a spontaneous exchange of population. Interviewer: "Spontaneous? You're playing a cruel joke. Seselj: "I'm not joking. The Muslims didn't want to stay and live under Serb control, and the Serbs did not want to stay under Muslim or Croat control. The Muslims were -- the Croats were expelling Serbs from the territory of West Herzegovina. The Muslims are hindering the exiting of Serbs from Sarajevo, Tuzla, and a few other places under their control, holding those Serbs hostages; that's their argument for insisting on a unitary state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The West will insist that people return to the houses they left, but only a few people will return because they feel unsafe. How could a family return when in their house there's already a family whose house was burned down. Those are very complicated things, which is good for the Americans, because they need a reason for a military presence." How did you code that record?

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: Well, I coded it as, again, "expulsion and exchange of population." And also "external threats to Serbs." But could I make a commentary on this particular --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ANTHONY OBERSCHALL
utterances.text: -- record? And this, again, is Dr. Seselj's thinking about the impossibility of actually restoring to their domiciles and properties of people who have been expelled or fled during warfare, as happened in -- in Bosnia. But actually what did take place after the Dayton Accords? An international commission was appointed which received applications for the restoration of properties of -- of people who had been expelled from wherever they -- or fled from wherever they had lived and -- and been kicked out of, and they were given an option -- well, this was a complicated process, because we're talking about seven, eight hundred thousand families in -- in that particular case, and it took a lot of time to -- to get a -- get a procedure and a quasi-judicial process working, but the commission essentially settled something, you know, like 95, 98 per cent of these cases. And a substantial minority of the displaced person and refugees decided to return to places where they are now a minority and eventually they got back their property and -- so the -- the process of restoring -- of giving people the option of returning, of having the populations that kicked them out having to accept them, to live with them again, and their properties being returned to them, has been rather successful. And I'd say is one of the positive achievements of the Dayton Accord. So it is -- you know, it is -- it is perfectly possible to do this. I mean, you can't really go back to exactly where you were at the start of these conflicts, but, you know, it can be done. And when Dr. Seselj says, "How could a family return when in their house there's already a family whose house was burnt down," well, in practice what happens is that the family whose house was burnt down and is now in a -- in a property also has a claim to being able to live in temporary quarters, get compensation, rebuild that house, vacate the property --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to stop you here. I'm going to stop you here, because it's now a quarter to 2.00 and there is another hearing after this one. Mrs. Dahl, according to my calculations, you have had something like two hours and 40 minutes. Therefore, tomorrow you will have one hour left. Is that enough time for you tomorrow, or would you need less than that?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I think that's a trick question to ask any lawyer if they'll take less time than they're given. Your Honour, I'm going to try to avoid the redundancy of these records and I will finish as expeditiously as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Just a piece of advice: You could gain some time by avoiding reading out the entire document. You could just give us the reference number of the document and then base your question on the document and take it from there. As you know, tomorrow we shall resume at 9.00 tomorrow morning in Courtroom II. The court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 12th day of December, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
